title: p-adic Hensel-lifting view: ES at p is a statement about the p-adic unit 4/p... no — about x,y,z with exactly one or two divisible by p (Type I/II)
connection: Type I: p | x only; write x = pX. Then 4/p = 1/(pX) + 1/y + 1/z ⟹ (4X − 1)/(pX) = 1/y + 1/z. So Type I ⟺ (4X−1)/(pX) is a two-term Egyptian fraction for some X. Type II: x = pX, y = pY: 4/p − 1/(pX) − 1/(pY) = (4XY − X − Y)/(pXY) = 1/z ⟹ z = pXY/(4XY − X − Y): Type II ⟺ (4XY − X − Y) | pXY. Since gcd(4XY−X−Y, XY) | ... these are the 'words' p = tuv − u − v? Let me not resolve; the item: make the X-parametrisations the primary object and study the p-adic valuations.
why: Explicit small-parameter forms (X, Y) make 'Type II ⟺ ∃ X,Y: (4XY − X − Y) | pXY' which with gcd analysis becomes 4XY − X − Y = p·(divisor of XY)/... The repo's word form p = tuv − u − v is this. Keep as the 'word' entry point for the free lane.
first_step: Derive carefully: Type II ⟺ ∃ X, Y ≥ 1 with (4XY − X − Y) | pXY; show this is equivalent to p = tuv − u − v with 4 | t (repo's statement) and record the dictionary.
refs: FRONTIER.md §1 words p = tuv − u − v

title: The word form p = tuv − u − v with t ∈ 4ℤ: 'every prime is tuv − u − v with 4 | t' as a multiplicative-additive representation problem
connection: p + u + v = tuv ⟺ p = (tu − 1)(tv − 1)/t − 1/t... i.e. tp + 1 = (tu − 1)(tv − 1). So with t = 4C: 4Cp + 1 = (4Cu − 1)(4Cv − 1) — the Type II divisor form exactly. So ES(p) ⟺ ∃ C: 4Cp+1 factors as a product of two numbers ≡ −1 mod 4C. This is 'a tied-modulus analogue of representing numbers as products in given classes'.
why: The representation 'N = ab with a ≡ b ≡ −1 mod m where m | N − 1' is a *symmetric* condition — N ≡ 1 mod m automatically; a ≡ −1 ⟹ b ≡ −1. The problem is exactly: for which N ≡ 1 (mod m) does N have a divisor ≡ −1 mod m? With N − 1 = 4Cp and m = 4C. The ES-specific twist is only 'N − 1 = m·p'.
first_step: Consider the generalised question G(m, k): does mk + 1 have a divisor ≡ −1 mod m? ES(p) is: ∃ m ≡ 0 mod 4 with G(m, p). Compute for each k ≤ 10⁴ the set of m with G(m,k) and look at its structure (e.g. is it always nonempty for m ≤ k^ε? for k not prime too?).

title: G(m, k) for composite k and the 'I3' census: every n > 2 433 600 is tuv − u − v with t,u,v ≥ 3
connection: Repo's I3 is the untied version (any t ≥ 3); ES needs t ∈ 4ℤ. The gap between 'some t ≥ 3' (proved for all large n? or census only?) and 't ≡ 0 mod 4' is a *congruence condition on one parameter* — maybe the I3 mechanism can be twisted by a character.
why: If I3 for all large n has a proof (not just census), the proof mechanism is the closest thing to ES; adding a congruence on t might be a 'character twist' of that proof.
first_step: git grep -n 'I3' FRONTIER.md ES_APPROACH_GENERATORS.md to see whether I3 is PROVED or CERTIFIED; if proved, read the proof and try the twist t ≡ 0 mod 4.

title: ES as a question about the multiplicative order structure of p modulo 4C: 'is −p a product of divisors of ...'
connection: From 4Cp + 1 = ab with a ≡ b ≡ −1 mod 4C: a ≡ −1 ⟹ ab ≡ 1 ✓ consistent. Alternative: fix a ≡ −1 mod 4C, a | 4Cp+1 ⟺ 4Cp ≡ −1 mod a ⟺ p ≡ −(4C)^{-1} mod a. So ES(p) ⟺ ∃ C, ∃ a ≡ −1 (mod 4C) with p ≡ −(4C)^{−1} (mod a). I.e., p lies in a specific residue class mod a, for some a ≡ −1 mod 4C. The union over (C, a) of these classes must cover all primes.
why: This is a covering system of residue classes {−(4C)^{−1} mod a : a ≡ −1 mod 4C} — with infinitely many moduli a. ES ⟺ the primes are covered by this explicit infinite system. 'Does an explicit infinite set of congruence classes cover all primes' is a question with tools (density of the union, Erdős's covering theory; and Hough-type minimum modulus results don't apply since moduli are unbounded).
first_step: Compute the density of integers (not just primes) covered by the classes with a ≤ A, as A grows; by inclusion–exclusion / sieve, is it 1 − O(1/log A)? Then which integers are uncovered (should include odd squares!).

title: Odd squares m² are uncovered by the (C, a) covering system — turn this into a *characterisation* of uncovered integers
connection: T1 says no Type I/II solutions at odd squares; in the covering language, m² ≡ −(4C)^{−1} mod a with a ≡ −1 mod 4C never holds (reciprocity). Ask: are odd squares the ONLY uncovered integers (together with the U(n) sporadics 105, 2961, 3985, 25305, 111969, 978145 — which concern a related but different U(n) statement; check which)? If the uncovered set is exactly {odd squares} ∪ finite, then ES is 'covering system misses exactly the squares', a Rickards–Stange-type statement.
why: This is the cleanest 'squares + sporadic' statement; it's a conjecture, but the structure (reciprocity makes squares fail) suggests the mechanism to prove coverage of non-squares is a 'quadratic reciprocity + something' argument.
first_step: Compute the uncovered set for n ≤ 10⁶ (all n, not just primes) under the Type II covering system (and separately Type I); compare with odd squares and the U(n) sporadics.

title: Reciprocity proof of T1 as a *template*: what is the exact Jacobi-symbol identity, and does its negation at non-squares produce a divisor?
connection: T1's proof: if m² = (ab − 1)/(4C) with a ≡ b ≡ −1 mod 4C then ... a Jacobi symbol contradiction. At a non-square p, the same Jacobi symbol computation gives no contradiction but gives *information* — e.g., a constraint on (−C/p) or (p/a) that must hold for any certificate; this constraint is a 'necessary condition' on winning C, and might be the thing to make sufficient.
why: Necessary conditions on winning C from reciprocity (e.g. 'C must satisfy (−C/p) = +1'?) halve the search space; verify whether such a condition is known and whether data confirms it.
first_step: Derive: from 4Cp + 1 = ab, a ≡ −1 mod 4C: compute (a/p)·(b/p) = (ab/p) = (1/p) = 1, and (p/a) via reciprocity... obtain a condition on C mod p or (C/p). Test numerically which Jacobi symbols are forced for winning (C, a).

title: Model theory: is ES expressible in a decidable theory after fixing the structure of (ℕ, +, ·|_{divisors of 4Cp+1})?
connection: Full arithmetic is undecidable, but fragments like Presburger + 'is a power of 2' (Büchi) or Skolem arithmetic (ℕ, ·) are decidable. ES mixes + and · minimally: 4Cp + 1 = ab, a ≡ b ≡ −1 (4C). Determine the weakest theory in which ES is expressible and whether any known decidability/undecidability result applies to its ∀∃ fragment.
why: Calibration: if ES lies in a decidable fragment, there's an algorithm to decide it (in principle); more realistically it identifies ES's logical complexity relative to e.g. Zaremba (also ∀∃ with bounded searches).
first_step: Write ES in the language (ℕ, +, ·, <) and try to reduce the number of multiplications; note that 'a ≡ −1 mod 4C' and 'ab = 4Cp+1' need two products with shared variables; check against the known decidable fragments (e.g. 'one multiplication' theories are already undecidable? — Robinson).

title: Nonstandard analysis: an ES counterexample would be a 'nonstandard prime' with no standard certificate — apply the transfer principle to the almost-all results
connection: In a nonstandard model, Vaughan's exceptional-set bound says exceptional primes are 'rare'; Loeb-measure arguments sometimes convert density statements into structural statements about all elements of a 'generic' nonstandard set (as in Jin's sumset theorems).
why: Jin used nonstandard methods to prove sumset structure results that were hard classically; the ES analogue would be a structure theorem for the (hypothetical) exceptional set. Low confidence.
first_step: Read Jin, 'Freiman's inverse problem with small doubling property' (Adv. Math 2007) for the method; think whether 'exceptional primes' can be shown to have a forbidden structure.
refs: R. Jin, nonstandard methods in additive combinatorics

title: Ergodic Ramsey: Furstenberg correspondence for the set of (C, a) certificates as a subset of ℕ² with positive density
connection: The set W = {(C, a) : a ≡ −1 mod 4C} has density 0 in ℕ² but positive 'logarithmic' density along C; ES says the map p ↦ (p mod a) hits a prescribed class in W for every p. Furstenberg's correspondence turns density into recurrence; multiple recurrence (Szemerédi-type) gives patterns in every positive-density set but says nothing about one specific p.
why: Probably a dead end, but 'ES for all p' resembles 'recurrence for every point' = topological dynamics (minimal systems), where pointwise results (Birkhoff, Hindman) exist. Is the ES certificate set a return-time set of a minimal system?
first_step: Formulate: R = {n : n has a certificate}; is R an IP-set or a thick/syndetic set? (Trivially syndetic since n ≡ 2,3 mod 4 always work.) Refine to primes: is the set of 'good C' syndetic in C for each fixed p? Check numerically whether gaps between winning C are bounded for fixed p.

title: Gaps between consecutive winning C at fixed p: bounded? polylog?
connection: For fixed p, the set of winning C is infinite (e.g. once one C wins, multiples? no — not obviously closed under multiplication; check). The gap structure of winning C's is a 1-D sequence per p whose 'syndeticity' would be a strong structural fact.
why: If winning C's for each p are syndetic with uniformly bounded gaps (say gap ≤ G for all p ≥ p₀), then 'some C ≤ G wins' — a bounded cover, which Mordell–Schinzel suggests is false for polynomial covers but maybe true as a non-polynomial fact. The data decides.
first_step: Compute winning C ≤ 10⁵ for 100 primes near 10⁶; measure max gap; check closure properties (is C winning ⟹ kC winning for some k's?).

title: Closure of winning C under multiplication: if 4Cp+1 = ab with a,b ≡ −1 mod 4C, what about C' = Ck?
connection: 4Ckp + 1 — relation to ab: 4Ckp + 1 = k(ab − 1) + 1 = kab − k + 1. No obvious divisor. But via the (x,y,z) form: a solution for p from C gives (x,y,z); scaling doesn't change C. So no direct closure; but the e-slice form (e ≡ −p mod 4) might have closure: if e works, does e·k work? Check.
why: Any closure property on the certificate set would be a group-like structure (cf. Markoff orbits); worth 10 minutes of computation.
first_step: For p ≤ 10⁴, list winning e-slices and winning C; test closure under multiplication by small k and under 'e ↦ 4N − e'-type involutions.

title: Involutions on the certificate set: swapping a ↔ b in 4Cp+1 = ab, and the (x,y,z) permutation symmetry
connection: Each Type II certificate (C, a, b) is unordered in {a,b}; each solution (x,y,z) has S₃ symmetry. Counting orbits rather than solutions might reveal parity structure (f(p) odd?) — Markoff's count mod p came from orbit sizes.
why: Parity of orbit counts is a classical trick for existence (e.g. Zagier's involution proof of two squares: an involution with exactly one fixed point ⟹ odd number of points ⟹ another involution has a fixed point). Can an involution on ES certificates with a *known* fixed point be built? Fixed points of a ↔ b: a = b ⟹ 4Cp+1 = a² ⟹ p = (a²−1)/(4C) = (a−1)(a+1)/(4C) — possible for specific (C, a)! E.g. a = 2C·k ± 1 ... with p prime: (a−1)(a+1) = 4Cp requires one of a ± 1 to be p times a small number. E.g. a = 2p ± 1? then (a−1)(a+1) = (2p)(2p ± 2) = 4p(p ± 1) so C = p ± 1 and a = 2p ± 1 ≡ −1 mod 4C? 2p+1 ≡ −1 mod 4(p+1) ⟺ 2p + 2 ≡ 0 mod 4p + 4 ✗. a = 2p − 1, C = p − 1: 2p − 1 ≡ −1 mod 4p − 4 ⟺ 2p ≡ 0 mod 4(p−1) ✗. Hmm. Try: is there ANY square certificate 4Cp + 1 = a² with a ≡ −1 mod 4C? a = 4Cu − 1: a² = 16C²u² − 8Cu + 1 = 4Cp + 1 ⟹ p = 4Cu² − 2u = 2u(2Cu − 1) — not prime unless u = 1, C: p = 2(2C − 1)... even. So no fixed points for primes. Still, Zagier-style involution bookkeeping could be set up on a larger set.
Involution-counting is the canonical 'rigidity' existence proof; even the failure analysis (no fixed points ⟹ even count ⟹ no info) is worth stating.
first_step: Define the full certificate set S_p = {(C, a, b)} for p ≤ 10⁴; compute |S_p| mod 2 (expect even) and look for another involution (e.g. (C, a, b) ↦ (C', a', b') via the Type I ↔ Type II relation) with a computable fixed-point set.

title: Hypergraph Turán / Erdős–Ko–Rado: the family of 'divisor sets in class' as an intersecting family
connection: Fix p. For each C, S_C = divisors of 4Cp+1 in class −1 mod 4C. The family {S_C} over C — are the sets pairwise 'related' (e.g. a divisor a of 4Cp+1 and a' of 4C'p+1 have gcd structure: gcd(4Cp+1, 4C'p+1) | (C − C')·4p... so gcd divides 4(C' − C))? That bounds how much two S_C can overlap — an 'almost disjointness' that makes the counting cleaner.
why: Near-disjointness of the certificate sets across C means the total count Σ|S_C| has small variance from overlaps — relevant to the second-moment approach and to 'at least one is nonempty' bookkeeping.
first_step: Prove gcd(4Cp+1, 4C'p+1) | 4(C−C')·… precisely; then the divisors in S_C ∩ S_{C'} are ≤ 4|C − C'| — tiny. Record the lemma.

title: Matroids / linear algebra over F₂: the 'sign vectors' of divisors of 4Cp+1 in (ℤ/4C)^×/squares
connection: (ℤ/4C)^× modulo squares is an F₂-vector space; prime factors of 4Cp+1 give vectors; −1 is a target vector; subset-product hits −1 in the quotient iff −1 ∈ span (a linear algebra question!). The full condition (−1 as a subset product, not mod squares) is harder, but the F₂-relaxation is linear and decidable by rank.
why: The F₂-relaxation is a necessary condition for a win that is *linear* — and its failure probability is exactly 2^{−(rank deficiency)}; it isolates the 'genus-like' part (characters of order 2) from the rest. Repo's 'genus layer is pointwise free' lemma may be this.
first_step: git grep -il 'genus layer' -- '*.md' and compare; then compute for p ≤ 10⁵, C ≤ 100: does the F₂-relaxation hold (−1 ∈ span of factor vectors mod squares) and how often does the full condition fail when the relaxation holds?

title: Higher-order relaxations: (ℤ/4C)^× modulo k-th powers for k = 4, 8 — a tower of linear relaxations
connection: Beyond the F₂ (genus) relaxation, consider the quotient by 4th powers (ℤ/4-modules, with 'Rédei symbols'); the Type-II condition mod 4th powers is a ℤ/4-linear condition. The repo has bsB_redei_oddpart; the tower idea is to see at which level the relaxation becomes 'tight' with the true condition.
why: If the condition becomes tight at a bounded level (e.g. mod 8th powers), ES reduces to a ℤ/8-linear statement about Rédei-type symbols — rigid, computable, and maybe provable via reciprocity laws of higher degree.
first_step: Compute, for p ≤ 10⁴, C ≤ 50: level k at which the 'k-th power relaxation' condition agrees with the true win/fail; histogram.

title: Representation theory: the count of divisors in class −1 mod 4C is a trace of a permutation representation
connection: #{d | N : d ≡ r mod m} = (1/φ(m)) Σ_χ χ̄(r) Σ_{d|N} χ(d); the inner sum is a 'twisted divisor function' σ₀(N, χ) which is the Fourier coefficient of an Eisenstein series E(χ, χ̄). Summing over C (with N = 4Cp+1, m = 4C) is summing coefficients of a *varying-level* Eisenstein family at the arguments 4Cp+1 — a 'horizontal' sum across levels.
why: Varying-level sums of Eisenstein coefficients have appeared in the theory of 'moments of L-functions over a family of levels' (e.g. Conrey–Iwaniec); positivity results for such family sums exist on average over the argument but here the argument is tied to the level.
first_step: Write Σ_{C≤X} σ₀(4Cp+1; χ_C-component) explicitly; look for a Petersson/Kuznetsov-type formula that handles 'argument = 4Cp+1 tied to level 4C'; search 'Eisenstein series coefficients at n ≡ 1 mod level'.

title: Theta correspondence / Siegel–Weil: representation numbers of p² by ternary forms as a positivity source
connection: Siegel–Weil gives representation numbers of quadratic forms as Eisenstein series values (positive main terms); ternary forms (3 variables) have local–global failures only at finitely many spinor exceptions. Type I: f·g = p² + 4c²d is a quaternary 'norm form' condition. Is there a ternary form Q with Q(c, …) = p² representation ⟺ a Type I certificate?
why: Representation by ternary forms with 'all large n represented' (Duke–Schulze-Pillot) is a proven pointwise theorem with log-size counts — close to ES's shape! It needs the form to be fixed; ES's 'form' varies with (c,d). Still, a fixed-form subfamily (e.g. d = 1 only) might inherit the theorem.
first_step: Fix d = 1: Type I with d = 1: f | p² + 4c² with f ≡ −p mod 4c. The equation p² + 4c² = fg with congruence — compare with representations of p² by the form x² + 4y² restricted by congruences; check whether Duke–Schulze-Pillot's theorem on 'all large n represented by a ternary form with congruence conditions' applies to some auxiliary ternary form.

title: Type I with d = 1 only: the 'sum of two squares' subfamily of ES
connection: Setting d = 1 in Type I gives p² + (2c)² = f·g with f ≡ −p (mod 4c). Since p ≡ 1 mod 4, p = u² + v² (Fermat); p² + 4c² = (p + 2ci)(p − 2ci) in ℤ[i] — f corresponds to an ideal divisor of (p + 2ci). The Gaussian integer structure is fully explicit: f = N(α) for α | p + 2ci. The congruence f ≡ −p mod 4c is then a condition on α mod 4c in ℤ[i].
why: This subfamily lives entirely in ℤ[i], where everything is computable via Gaussian factorisation; a complete analysis (which p have a d=1 Type I solution? density? structure of failures?) is a clean sub-problem; failures are the input to the general problem.
first_step: Compute the set of p ≤ 10⁷ with no d=1 Type I solution for c ≤ 10⁴; density, structure (do they correlate with p's Gaussian factorisation u + vi?).

title: Kronecker's limit formula / class number h(−4d) as the 'main term' for Type I at fixed d
connection: Σ_c #{f | p² + 4c²d, f ≡ −p (4cd)} over c ≤ X is a sum over representations by forms of discriminant −16d... whose total is controlled by class numbers; Kronecker–Hurwitz-type formulas give Σ_c r_Q(p² + 4c²d) in terms of h(−d·) and L(1, χ).
why: Exact class-number formulas are 'rigid' inputs; if the Type I count at fixed d has a class-number main term with an explicit error, choosing d with large h(−4d)/√d (many classes, small discriminant) maximises the main term.
first_step: For d ∈ {1, 2, 3, 5, 7} compute the Type I count over c ≤ X numerically for p ≈ 10⁶ and compare with h(−4d)·log X·const; estimate the constant.

title: Eichler–Selberg trace formula: Hurwitz class numbers H(4p − t²) sum to traces of Hecke operators — does an ES count hide in a trace?
connection: Σ_t H(4p − t²) = (traces of T_p on cusp forms) + explicit terms (Eichler–Selberg). ES-type counts involve divisors of p² + 4c²d = discriminant-like quantities −(p² + 4c²d) = disc of forms? For Type I, 4c²d + p² ≡ p² mod 4 ≡ 1 mod 4... hmm, −(p² + 4c²d) ≡ 3 mod 4 is a valid negative discriminant! So Type I involves H(p² + 4c²d)-type class numbers summed over c — resembling Σ_t H(4n − t²) with roles of t and n changed (t ↔ p fixed, n ↔ varying c).
why: If Σ_c H(p² + 4c²d) over c in an AP equals a trace of a Hecke operator at p on some space (via a 'reversed' Eichler–Selberg), then positivity/non-vanishing of traces (Deligne bounds give |tr T_p| ≤ (dim)·2p^{(k−1)/2}; not positivity) — more usefully, the trace formula gives an *exact* identity which might convert a 'divisor in class' count into a modular-form coefficient count.
first_step: Search 'Hurwitz class numbers H(p² + 4m) sum' and 'class number sums over quadratic polynomials'; check Eichler–Selberg with weight/level to see if Σ_m H(p² + 4m) (m in an AP) is a known trace.
refs: Zagier, 'Nombres de classes et formes modulaires de poids 3/2'

title: Mock modular forms / Zagier's weight-3/2 Eisenstein series for class-number generating functions evaluated at the ES data
connection: The generating function Σ H(n)q^n is a mock modular form (Zagier). The ES Type I count relates to H(p² + 4c²d) (previous item). Mock modularity gives asymptotics with *explicit* error terms for sums of H over quadratic sequences (via holomorphic projection / shadow).
why: Explicit error terms for 'class numbers along quadratic sequences p² + 4c²d in c' might, for a single p, give a positive main term exceeding the error — a pointwise statement! The size: main term ≍ X·√(p)... vs ES's count log²p — the class-number sum counts ALL divisors, not the residue-class-constrained ones; the constraint costs 1/φ(4cd), summing to ≈ log X. So the error term must be < log X — hopeless unless the error is tiny. Record the calculation.
first_step: Compute Σ_{c ≤ X} H(p² + 4c²) for p = 10⁶+3 and compare with main term; then the constrained count; tabulate the ratio.

title: Knot theory: continued fractions ↔ rational tangles (Conway); 'ES₅ CF length ≤ 3' as a tangle with ≤ 3 twists
connection: Rational tangles are classified by continued fractions; a rational number with CF length ≤ 3 corresponds to a 3-twist tangle; 2-bridge knots are classified by p/q with CF structure. ES₅ asks that a p-tied rational has CF length ≤ 3 — a topological statement about a 2-bridge link family.
why: Pure translation, but 2-bridge link invariants (Alexander polynomial, signature, Rasmussen) are computable from p/q and might encode CF length in a way with a known 'all-p' theorem (e.g. a signature formula via Dedekind sums).
first_step: Write the ES₅ rational r_p (FRONTIER §1); for p ≤ 1000 compute the 2-bridge link K(r_p) and its signature; see whether 'length ≤ 3' corresponds to a computable invariant threshold.
refs: Kauffman–Lambropoulou, 'On the classification of rational tangles'

title: Lens spaces L(p, q) and the CF form: ES₅ ⟺ a specific lens space has a surgery/plumbing description with ≤ 3 vertices
connection: L(p,q) bounds a linear plumbing whose length is the CF length of p/q (Hirzebruch–Jung); repo has bsA_lens_homotopy_surgery. ES₅'s 'λ ≤ 3' is 'the plumbing has ≤ 3 vertices'. Topological invariants (d-invariants, Casson–Walker) may bound CF length.
why: Already in repo; the free-lane addition: ask for a *lower-bound-free* argument: is there a topological reason a specific family of lens spaces (indexed by p via ES's rational) has short plumbings? Probably not, but lens-space surgery realisation theorems (Greene) are rigid and all-p.
first_step: git grep -il 'lens' BRAINSTORM | head; read bsA_lens_homotopy_surgery.md; check whether Greene's lens space realisation (which lens spaces arise from integer surgery on knots in S³) applies to ES's family.
refs: Greene, 'The lens space realization problem' (Ann. Math 2013)

title: Apollonian circle packings: curvatures satisfy 'local-global' with finitely many exceptions (Bourgain–Kontorovich) — the proof shape for 'all large n in admissible classes'
connection: Bourgain–Kontorovich (and the 2023 Haag–Kertzer–Rickards–Stange disproof of full local-global for Apollonian packings via reciprocity!) are a very ES-like story: a reciprocity obstruction (quadratic/quartic) kills some admissible classes. The repo has apollonian_reciprocity.md. The free-lane item: the HKRS *reciprocity obstruction* is a mechanism that FINDS missing curvatures; apply the same reciprocity analysis to ES to see whether it predicts non-square failures (a disproof route) or shows squares are the only obstruction.
why: HKRS's method is exactly 'use quadratic reciprocity on the Descartes quadratic form to show a residue class is missed'; for ES, the same analysis on the Type I/II forms should reproduce T1 and either find more or show T1 is all.
first_step: Read HKRS 'The local-global conjecture for Apollonian circle packings is false' §3 (reciprocity obstructions), then run the same style of argument on 4Cp+1 = ab with a ≡ b ≡ −1 (4C): list all quadratic/quartic obstructions.

title: Quartic reciprocity obstructions: does ES have a hidden quartic obstruction at non-squares (p = m⁴ + …)?
connection: HKRS found both quadratic and *quartic* reciprocity obstructions in Apollonian packings. For ES, T1 is quadratic (odd squares). A quartic analogue would obstruct some class of non-squares — contradicting ES (verified to 10¹⁸), so it must not exist for Type I+II combined; but it might exist for Type I alone or Type II alone, explaining the U(n) sporadics or Type-separated failures.
why: If a quartic obstruction forces f_I(p) = 0 for an infinite explicit set of p, then ES for those p rests entirely on Type II — a sharpening of where the difficulty is; also a consistency check of the repo's claim f_I ≥ 1 for all p ≤ 10⁸.
first_step: Check numerically: among p ≤ 10⁸ (repo data), is there any p with f_I(p) = 0 or f_II(p) = 0? (FRONTIER says none.) Then look for p where f_I is anomalously small relative to f_II and test quartic residue symbols (2/p)_4, (−1/p)_4 as predictors.

title: Markoff-type 'orbit size divisible by p' — is there any natural group action on ES certificates with orbit sizes forced by p?
connection: Chen's Markoff proof: Γ-orbits on X*(p) have size ≡ 0 mod p; since |X*(p)| is known mod p, there must be... The ES analogue needs a group acting on certificates. Candidates: (ℤ/4C)^× acting on divisors by multiplication (doesn't preserve 'divisor of N'); Galois group acting on ideal factors in ℤ[√−d] (Type I) — orbits of size 1 or 2 only.
why: Negative-ish: list exhaustively the natural actions and their orbit sizes; the absence of any p-sized orbit structure is a clear statement of why Markoff's method doesn't transfer, and any surprise would be a lead.
first_step: Write the list: S₃ on (x,y,z); a ↔ b; Galois in ℤ[√−d]; Atkin–Lehner-type involutions on the level 4C; check whether composing them gives an action with orbit size related to p.

title: Noncommutative: quaternion orders of discriminant tied to p — the repo's quaternion reformulation and the 'Eichler mass formula' as a positive main term
connection: Repo lists quaternion orders. Eichler's mass formula gives Σ 1/|O_i^×| = explicit (positive) sum over classes; representation numbers of orders are theta-series coefficients. If ES certificates are 'optimal embeddings' of a quadratic order into a quaternion order (as in Eichler's embedding theory), the count is a product of local embedding numbers × class number — exactly a formula with a positive main term.
why: Optimal-embedding counts are *exact* (Eichler) when summed over the genus; the pointwise count for one maximal order has a spectral error (Gross–Zagier-type). Positivity for one order at level p... the 'one order' is the issue (B2 again), but the embedding-number formula may reveal which local conditions matter.
first_step: git grep -il quaternion -- '*.md' and read the repo's reformulation; then check whether Type I/II certificates are optimal embeddings of ℤ[√−d]-type orders into a definite quaternion order of discriminant related to p or 4C.
refs: Gross, 'Heights and the special values of L-series'

title: Gross–Zagier / Waldspurger: the count of certificates as a toric period, nonvanishing ⟺ L(1/2) ≠ 0
connection: If the certificate count is a sum of a theta-type function over a torus orbit (CM points), Waldspurger's formula expresses |sum|² as L(1/2, f × χ) — nonvanishing of L-values implies nonvanishing of the count. Non-vanishing of L(1/2) for *every* twist in a family is open in general, but for specific families (e.g. by Goldfeld's conjecture) it holds for 'most'.
why: Converts ES-like positivity into L-value nonvanishing — a well-studied (if hard) target with GRH-conditional results (one nonvanishing twist among polylog many). Need the dictionary.
first_step: Formulate: is Σ_{d | 4Cp+1} χ(d) (χ of order 2 mod 4C with χ(−1) = −1) a toric period of an Eisenstein series? (Eisenstein, not cuspidal — then Waldspurger is replaced by Hecke's formula for L(s, χ)L(s, χ') — which is explicit!) Compute: the twisted divisor sum Σ_{d|N} χ(d) = coefficient of E(χ,1); positivity of this coefficient at N = 4Cp+1 is the question; it factors over primes q | N as Π (1 + χ(q) + … ); it's zero iff some prime q ∥ N has χ(q) = −1 … so the sign structure is completely explicit per C. Document.

title: Per-C exact sign structure: #{d | N, d ≡ −1 (m)} as a combination of multiplicative functions — the explicit product formula
connection: For m = 4C, #{d | N : d ≡ r (m)} = (1/φ(m)) Σ_χ χ̄(r) Π_{q^e ∥ N} (1 + χ(q) + … + χ(q)^e). For N = 4Cp + 1 ≡ 1 mod m the trivial character contributes τ(N)/φ(m); each nontrivial χ contributes χ̄(−1)·Π(...). ES(p) fails at C iff these cancel exactly to 0. 'Exact cancellation of a sum of φ(m) products' is a strong algebraic condition.
why: The exact-cancellation view suggests an algebraic-number-theoretic approach: the sum is an algebraic integer in ℚ(ζ_{φ(m)})… no, it's rational; but the Π over characters is a norm-like expression. Cancellation to 0 might be ruled out by a *valuation* argument (2-adic valuation of τ(N)/φ(m) vs the rest) for suitable C — a rigidity mechanism!
first_step: Compute the 2-adic valuation of the trivial-character term τ(N)/φ(4C) and of the sum of nontrivial terms for failing (p, C); check whether failures require specific 2-adic coincidences; if a C with v₂-mismatch always exists, that's a proof direction.

title: Analytic continuation trick: define F_p(s) = Σ_C C^{−s} · #{d | 4Cp+1, d ≡ −1 (4C)} and study its pole/residue at s = 1
connection: If F_p(s) has a simple pole at s = 1 with residue R(p) > 0 computable from local data, then infinitely many C win (for each p) — ES(p) with a vengeance. The residue would come from the 'main term' of the C-average, which the campaign computes as M_BM. The question is whether F_p(s) continues and whether the residue is provably positive — i.e., whether a *Tauberian* argument works at fixed p.
why: Tauberian arguments at fixed p would be a new shape: the Dirichlet series in C at fixed p is a 'vertical' object (like a Dirichlet series of a shifted-divisor problem Σ τ(4Cp+1)C^{−s}, which DOES continue meromorphically with a pole at s=1 — Estermann/Ingham-type). The residue-class restriction d ≡ −1 (4C) is the new feature.
first_step: Study the simpler series Σ_C τ(4Cp+1)C^{−s} (known: continuation via Estermann's treatment of Σ τ(an+b)n^{−s}); then insert the character condition and see if the continuation survives with an explicit residue.

title: Shifted divisor problem at fixed shift p: Σ_{C ≤ X} τ(4Cp+1) with X ≪ p^ε — the 'short range' regime
connection: Classical: Σ_{n ≤ X} τ(an + b) ~ (main) for X ≫ a^{1+ε} or so; ES needs C only up to polylog(p) ideally (so X ≪ a^ε, far below the classical range). In the short range, the sum is dominated by the structure of the specific p — i.e. exactly the pointwise regime. Known results: for X ≥ a^{1/2+ε}? (Friedlander–Iwaniec, divisor function in APs to large moduli; Fouvry). For X < a^{1/2} essentially nothing is known pointwise.
why: Pins down the exact analytic barrier: ES(p) with C ≤ p^θ requires understanding τ(4Cp+1)-type sums with C ≤ p^θ; θ < 1/2 is beyond current technology for the *unrestricted* divisor sum, let alone the class-restricted one. But θ ≥ 1 (C up to p) IS within technology for the unrestricted sum — so 'ES with C ≤ p' might be attackable via large-modulus divisor results if the class restriction can be handled by characters (log-many characters…).
first_step: Read Fouvry–Iwaniec / Friedlander–Iwaniec on τ in APs to moduli q ≤ x^{2/3}; map to Σ_{C ≤ X} τ(4Cp + 1) with p as the 'modulus' and X as the range: need X ≥ p^{3/2}? Record the exact requirement.
refs: Friedlander–Iwaniec, 'Incomplete Kloosterman sums and a divisor problem' (Ann. Math 1985)

title: ES with large C (C up to p or p²): is the problem *easier* with a power-size reservoir, and does it still imply something?
connection: ES(p) only needs ONE C; nothing stops C from being huge. With C ≤ p^A the number of candidate C is p^A, the expected number of wins Σ_{C ≤ p^A} 1/φ(4C)·(…) ≈ A log p — still log! (Each C wins with probability ~1/φ(4C)... no wait: probability that 4Cp+1 has a divisor ≡ −1 mod 4C is roughly (number of divisors)/φ(4C) ≈ log(4Cp)/(4C)… so Σ_C log(Cp)/C ≈ log p · log X.) So count ≈ log p · log X even with X = p^A — logarithmic in X, confirming B3 for Type II. BUT in the e-slice/Type I forms, parameters (c, d) are two-dimensional: #(c,d) ≤ X² with win-probability 1/φ(4cd)·τ — Σ_{c,d ≤ X} τ(p² + 4c²d)/(4cd) ≈ log p · log²X. Still polylog. Confirms: no power reservoir in any parametrisation. Record as a calibration item.
why: Documents rigorously that every parametrisation has a polylog expected count regardless of the range; useful as a lemma for the 'generator matrix'.
first_step: Write the expected-count computation for Type I, Type II, and e-slice forms with ranges up to p^A; confirm polylog; check against ES_APPROACH_GENERATORS §B3.

title: Weighted counts: instead of counting certificates, weight each by a function w(C, a) chosen to make the sum provably positive
connection: Counting with weights w ≥ 0 that vanish on 'hard' regions can make the error term smaller relative to the main term; Selberg-sieve weights (λ_d) are the classical example, and Maynard's multi-dimensional weights broke the bounded-gaps problem. For ES: weight certificates by smoothness of a, by C^{−s}, by Legendre-symbol filters.
why: Weight optimisation is a standard move that changed outcomes in sieve theory; the ES count has never (?) been weighted beyond C^{−s}.
first_step: Define a parametrised weight family (e.g. w = Λ-type weights on C or on a) and numerically compute the ratio (weighted count)/(its p-average) for p ≤ 10⁶; find weights minimising the spread of the ratio (i.e. maximising concentration), then analyse the best one.

title: Erdős–Rényi random graph threshold: at what 'connectivity' does the prime–template bipartite graph lose isolated vertices?
connection: An isolated prime (no template among those used by primes ≤ X) is a 'locally unique' solver; the growth of the number of isolated primes vs X measures the entropy of the solution structure.
why: If isolated primes vanish (every prime shares a template with another), the templates form a 'cover with reuse', a weak form of structure.
first_step: Build the bipartite graph (primes ≤ 10⁶, templates = (C, a mod 4C) or (c,d)); count isolated vertices as a function of X.

title: Design theory: do winning (C, a)-pairs form a block design over residue classes of p mod M?
connection: A covering design covers all k-subsets by blocks; here, blocks = {p mod M : (C, a) wins} for each (C, a); ES = covering of all prime residues. The 'covering number' structure of the block system might have a design-theoretic description (e.g. it's a union of cosets of subgroups of (ℤ/M)^×).
why: Design-theoretic regularity (each residue covered equally often) is exactly the kind of structure a uniform argument needs; irregularity points at hard residues.
first_step: For M = 840, compute for each residue r the number of (C, a) pairs with C ≤ 50 that win for ALL primes ≡ r (i.e. polynomial identities) and for a positive fraction; display as a matrix.

title: Analogy of analogy: ES ↔ Zaremba ↔ Markoff ↔ Apollonian — the 'thin orbit' quadrilateral; where does ES sit in the (orbit, expansion, obstruction) triangle?
connection: Zaremba (solved, claimed): thin semigroup orbit, expansion, no obstruction. Markoff mod p: group orbit, expansion, divisibility rigidity. Apollonian: thin group orbit, expansion, reciprocity obstruction (local-global FALSE). ES: no known group/semigroup, polylog count, reciprocity obstruction at squares. The missing ingredient is the orbit; the free-lane question: can ES certificates be realised as a thin *semigroup* orbit in SL₂(ℤ) or in a 2×2×2 cube structure, with p as a 'level'?
why: Pattern-matching across the four problems isolates exactly one missing ingredient (an orbit structure) — a concrete target for construction rather than proof.
first_step: Write the ES₅ CF form as a product of SL₂(ℤ) generators (Zaremba-style: p/q with partial quotients ≤ A ⟺ matrix in a semigroup orbit); identify what plays the role of 'q' and whether ES is 'λ ≤ 3' for a rational with *p-tied* numerator — then it's a *level* condition, not an orbit condition. Document the mismatch precisely.

title: Semigroup orbit reformulation: Type II certificates as products of two 'elementary' matrices in a congruence semigroup
connection: 4Cp + 1 = (4Cu − 1)(4Cv − 1). Consider matrices M_C(u) = [[4Cu − 1, ?],[?, ?]] in SL₂? E.g. the matrix [[4Cu−1, −u],[−4C·?..]] — find a representation where the product M_C(u)·M_C(v) has p as an entry. Try: A_u = [[1, u],[0, 1]]·[[1, 0],[−4C, 1]]·... Standard: the continued fraction [0; 4C, u, ...]? Let's just make it an experiment.
why: If Type II certificates are entries of products in a 2-generator semigroup (parametrised by C), then 'p appears as an entry' is a thin-orbit problem with the level 4C — same shape as Zaremba (where the semigroup is fixed and q is the entry). The novelty: the semigroup depends on C, but p must appear for SOME C — a union over C of thin orbits.
first_step: Find matrices in SL₂(ℤ) whose (1,1)-entry of a length-2 product is (4Cu−1)(4Cv−1) − 1)/(4C) = p for integers u,v (e.g. [[4Cu−1, u],[4C·?, ?]] with det 1 forces entries); if found, compare with the ES₅ word of length 3.

title: Bourgain–Kontorovich-style 'local-global for a thin semigroup orbit' in the C-direction: fix p, vary (u, v): p = 4Cuv − u − v
connection: Rewrite p = 4Cuv − u − v ⟹ for fixed C this is a quadratic form in (u, v) (indefinite: 4Cuv − u − v); p is represented by the 'form' Q_C(u,v) = 4Cuv − u − v for some C. Representation of p by one of a family of indefinite binary quadratic polynomials — a family of *quadratic* problems, each with a class-group structure (indefinite forms: Pell-type unit group acts on representations!).
why: For fixed C, representations of p by 4Cuv − u − v: complete the square: (4Cu − 1)(4Cv − 1) = 4Cp + 1; so it's the divisor problem again — but the INDEFINITE FORM viewpoint says: the 'automorphs' of the form act on solutions; the form 4Cuv − u − v has discriminant (4C)² — a *square* discriminant, so the form is degenerate (a product of linear forms) and its automorph group is trivial. OK so no Pell action — that's why no orbit. Document: 'the ES form has square discriminant; its automorph group is trivial; hence no Vieta/Pell dynamics'. This is a clean statement of the missing orbit.
first_step: Write it up as a lemma: every ES parametrisation (Type I, Type II, e-slice) has a quadratic form of square discriminant ⟹ no infinite automorphism group ⟹ no orbit dynamics. Check Type I: f·g = p² + 4c²d with f ≡ −p mod 4cd — discriminant of the relevant form is −16c²d, NOT square — so Type I does have a class group (finite, ℚ(√−d)) but no infinite unit group. So the only rigid structure is the finite class group of ℚ(√−d), varying with d.

title: Use the finite class group of ℚ(√−d) at Type I: choose d so that the class group is trivial (d ∈ {1,2,3,7,11,19,43,67,163}) and the divisor condition becomes a *splitting* condition
connection: For class number 1 fields, ideals = elements; f | p² + 4c²d with f ≡ −p (mod 4cd) ⟺ p + 2c√−d = α·β in O_d with N(α) = f and a congruence on N(α). For h = 1, α is an actual element, so f = N(α) = s² + d t² (or the appropriate norm form) with a congruence on s² + dt² mod 4cd AND α | p + 2c√−d. This makes Type I at Heegner d's completely explicit in terms of representations of p + 2c√−d's divisors.
why: The nine Heegner discriminants give nine fully explicit sub-problems; Type I failures at all nine simultaneously would be a strong constraint on p; maybe the nine cases 'cover' primes by a non-polynomial reason (e.g., p's splitting pattern in the 9 fields = 9 Legendre symbols ⟹ 2⁹ profiles).
first_step: For each Heegner d and p ≤ 10⁶, compute whether a Type I solution with that d exists (c ≤ 10³); tabulate the 9-bit failure vector; check if any profile has all 9 failing.
refs: Cox, Primes of the form x² + ny²

title: ES for primes in a fixed Chebotarev class of a big compositum: a 'conditional on splitting' infinite family
connection: Fix the splitting of p in K = ℚ(i, √2, √3, √5, √7, …) (finitely many Legendre symbols); for a given profile, does a *fixed* Type I/II template (with d, c chosen by the profile) always work? That would be an identity depending on Legendre symbols — not polynomial, so not excluded by Mordell–Schinzel.
why: Legendre-symbol-dependent identities are a natural, unexplored (?) class strictly larger than polynomial identities. Even partial coverage (e.g. all profiles except those where p is a square mod all small primes — which includes squares!) would be a beautiful structural statement matching T1.
first_step: For primes ≤ 10⁷ with profile (p mod 840, (p/q) for q ≤ 31), check whether the first winning template (C, a mod 4C) is constant on the profile class; count profile classes with a constant template.

title: Primes that are squares modulo all small primes (pseudo-squares, Lehmer) as the 'hardest' profile for ES — test them
connection: Pseudosquares (Lehmer): integers ≡ 1 mod 8 that are QRs mod all primes ≤ q but not squares. Primes that are pseudosquares 'look like squares' to all small Legendre symbols; if ES solutions come from Legendre-symbol identities, pseudosquare primes are where they fail — they are the natural adversarial family.
why: Sharp test family; tables of pseudosquares exist (up to ~10²⁵ for q ≤ 373, Sorenson et al.).
first_step: Fetch the pseudosquare table (OEIS A002189); for each prime pseudosquare, compute f(p), C_min(p); compare to controls of the same size.

title: Does ES hold for the square-like composites m² + 24k with small k? (near-square test)
connection: Odd squares are the obstruction for Type I/II; integers *near* squares in the Legendre-profile sense (QR mod many primes) or in size (m² + small) are the natural 'almost obstruction' test; if f(m² + 24) is systematically small, the obstruction has a 'continuity' which a proof would need to respect.
why: Empirical probe of 'how localised' T1 is.
first_step: Compute f(n) for n = m² + 24k, k = 1..5, m ≤ 10⁴ (n not necessarily prime; use Type I/II counts); compare with random n of the same size.

title: Composite n and the 'certificate from a factor' loophole: ES(n) for n = pq follows from ES(p); but are there composites with NO Type I/II solution other than squares and the sporadics?
connection: The U(n) list (105, 2961, 3985, 25305, 111969, 978145) are exactly such sporadics (for the U(n) statement). Understanding WHY 105 = 3·5·7 fails the direct Type I/II test while 3, 5, 7 each succeed — a 'non-transfer' of certificates to products — is a small concrete structure question.
why: Sporadics are the fingerprints of the mechanism; their factorisations (105 = 3·5·7; 2961 = 3²·7·47; 3985 = 5·797; 25305 = 3·5·7·241; 111969 = 3·37·1009? check; 978145 = 5·...?) might share a pattern (many small primes ≡ 3 mod 4? products of a square and something?).
first_step: Factor all six sporadics; compute their Legendre profiles; list which small C fail and why (subgroup type or few factors); see if a common structural reason emerges.

title: ES over ℤ[1/2] or ℤ[1/6] (allowing denominators with small prime powers freely): does the problem become covered by identities?
connection: Relaxing integrality at 2 and 3 (S-integers) might make the odd-square obstruction disappear (T1 uses parity structure mod 4) and allow a complete identity cover; comparing the S-integral and integral problems isolates the role of the prime 2.
why: If ES over ℤ[1/2] is a theorem (by covering), then the entire difficulty of ES is '2-adic' — focusing the problem.
first_step: Formulate ES over ℤ[1/2]: 4/n = 1/x + 1/y + 1/z with x,y,z ∈ ℤ[1/2]_{>0}; multiply through: equivalent to 4·2^k/n = ... for some k, i.e. ES for 2^k·n / ... hmm: 4/n = Σ 2^{a_i}/x_i' — i.e. 'Egyptian fractions with numerators powers of 2' — a known variant? Search 'unit fractions numerators powers of two'.

title: Dual problem: 4/n as a sum of three unit fractions with *negative* signs allowed (Pierce-type): 4/n = 1/x + 1/y − 1/z
connection: Allowing one negative term is much easier (presumably always solvable by identities); the exact boundary between 'sign-mixed solvable by identities' and 'all-positive open' isolates what positivity costs.
why: Comparing the mixed-sign problem's identity cover with Mordell's reveals which identities are 'lost' to positivity — maybe a single family, which would be the one to replace.
first_step: Find/prove a covering of all n by identities for 4/n = 1/x + 1/y − 1/z; then for each Mordell class, note which mixed-sign identity covers the square classes and why its positive version fails.

title: Count of representations with multiplicity: Σ_{solutions} 1 vs Σ_{solutions} 1/(stabiliser) — Siegel-mass-style weighted counts might be more 'modular'
connection: Siegel's mass formula is exact for weighted counts (by 1/|Aut|); for ES, 'automorphisms' are permutations of equal coordinates; weighting by 1/|Stab| makes f(n) a 'mass'. If the mass has an exact formula (e.g. a divisor-sum identity) for some sub-count, that's rigid structure.
why: Checking whether any ES sub-count satisfies an exact identity (like r₂(n) = 4Σ χ₄(d)) is cheap and would be a major structural discovery.
first_step: Compute the Type II mass m_II(n) = Σ 1/|Stab| for n ≤ 10⁴; test multiplicativity, test against OEIS, test linear relations with τ(n), σ(n), r₂(n), h(−4n).

title: Is f_II(n) (or any ES count) a *multiplicative* or 'quasi-multiplicative' function?
connection: Egyptian-fraction counts are not multiplicative (solutions for pq are not products of solutions for p and q), but there may be a sub-count (e.g. 'primitive' Type II certificates, coprimality-restricted) that is multiplicative or satisfies a Hecke-type relation f(pq) = f(p)f(q) + correction.
why: Multiplicativity would make f a Dirichlet-series coefficient with an Euler product — immediate structure; Hecke-type relations would be modular-form-like.
first_step: Compute f_II(n) for n ≤ 10⁴ and test f(mn) vs f(m)f(n) for coprime m,n; look for a correction term pattern.

title: Category-theoretic / functorial view: ES as a natural transformation between the functors n ↦ Div(4Cn+1) and n ↦ residue classes
connection: Half-joke, half-meta: which constructions are *natural in n*? Polynomial identities are natural transformations ℤ[n] → solutions; Mordell–Schinzel says no natural transformation exists on square classes. The question becomes: what is the weakest 'naturality' (e.g. natural in the category of ℤ with Legendre-symbol decorations) that admits a solution map?
why: Organises the 'what kind of identity' question by the structure the identity is allowed to see (polynomial / Legendre symbols / factorisation of 4Cn+1 / full factorisation of n). A hierarchy of 'identity types' with the known no-go results placed on it is a useful map.
first_step: Write the hierarchy: (0) polynomial in n; (1) polynomial in n and ⌊√n⌋; (2) depending on n mod M for bounded M (= covering); (3) depending on Legendre symbols of n w.r.t. bounded primes; (4) depending on the factorisation of 4Cn+1 for bounded C; (5) unbounded. Place Mordell–Schinzel at (0), and ask which level ES's known data refutes.

title: Reciprocity-law zoo: Eisenstein reciprocity, Rédei symbols, Hilbert symbols — which one is T1 'really', and do its cousins give conditions at non-squares?
connection: T1 is proved by quadratic reciprocity; but the structure 'square ⟹ all certificates vanish' might be a special case of a reciprocity for a 4-term symbol (Rédei) or a Hilbert-symbol product formula (Π_v (a,b)_v = 1). The product formula is an *exact* global identity — if the ES certificate count mod 2 equals a Hilbert symbol product at some place, that's a parity theorem.
why: Parity theorems from the product formula are the standard rigid mechanism in 2-descent; ES's count mod 2 is unexplored (item on involutions).
first_step: Compute f_II(p) mod 2 and f_I(p) mod 2 for p ≤ 10⁶; test against Hilbert symbols (−1, p)_2, (2, p)_2, (p, −C)_q for small C, q; look for an exact parity formula.
